title: The Whole Ten Yards
full_review:
A pathetically unfunny comedy sequel if ever there was one, "The Whole Ten Yards" (Warner Bros.) isn't satisfied with being dumb, noisy, badly written and hammily acted. It takes pains to offend Catholics with its mocking sensibility.

At issue is main character Jimmy Tudeski (Bruce Willis), who's killed 21 people, staged his own death and now lives luxuriously in Mexico with wife Jill (Amanda Peet), who is desperate to follow in his footsteps as an assassin. She's miserable that her targets keep dying before she can pull the trigger.

Up shows dentist Oz (Matthew Perry) whose falsified dental records helped fake Jimmy's death. Oz warns the couple that mobster Gogolak (Kevin Pollak) is out of the pen, sure that Jimmy's alive, and on the trail to find and kill him. The mobster's also holding Oz's wife, Cynthia (Natasha Henstridge), hostage, and she just happened to be Jimmy's first wife as well.

After Jimmy affirms he is a "devout Catholic" and Oz reveals that Cynthia gave Jimmy the prominent gold cross he always wears around his neck, Jill goes into a jealous rage. At first downplaying his crucifix as "just a good-luck charm," Jimmy later refuses to take it off as "it represents my Lord and Savior." He makes much of being Catholic, weeping that God may not want him to become a father since he's a mass murderer, although he shows zero remorse for having ended so many lives. And, as the movie progresses, Jimmy has little trouble going back to his killing and robbing ways.

Director Howard Deutch seems to think that with enough scenery chewing by Pollak and Willis, coupled with flying bullets and disposable crooks, perhaps the barren script won't be so obvious. The 2000 original, "The Whole Nine Yards," may have had some genuine laughs but this lame sequel is bereft of any wit and not shy about trashing a religious symbol sacred to much of the audience.

In the final scene, flush with millions in dirty money and a pregnant wife, Willis' character rips off his crucifix, smugly remarking, "I don't need this anymore." Well, guess what, Bruce -- Christians don't need your insulting movie either.

Due to its glamorization of crime, jokey treatment of deadly violence, sexual situations, rear nudity, and an instance of profanity and rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
